author: haiku
reason: Document A is tighter and has one clear layout: one diagram for the flows, numbered rules for the mechanics, the schema, and a single table for every storage failure. Document B spreads its failure handling across a dense decisions table, the diagram and a separate rules section, and it pads that with definitions a technical reader doesn't need, which slows the reader down.

author: haiku
reason: B is the faster read for a smart engineer: a compact diagram, the actual expiry SQL and schema, a named middleware check, and a storage-failure table organised by where the failure happens, while A spreads the same flow across a long glossary of basic terms, a large decisions table and a separate rules section.

author: sonnet
reason: A sets out each flow (login, protected request, logout, cleanup) as numbered steps, defines its terms first and puts all failure cases in one table, while B spreads the same flow across topic sections and ends with a requirements table numbered against a brief the reader has never seen.

author: sonnet
reason: B opens with a one-paragraph main flow and short definitions, then walks login, protected request and logout as numbered steps, with a separate failure table; A spreads the same behavior across topic bullets, so a newcomer has to rebuild the request flow from the diagram.

author: haiku
reason: A runs as nine steps in one straight order, says up front how they group, and puts the startup sequence and its failure handling in one place, while B spreads the flow over 19 steps with stated exceptions to the numeric order (16-17 before 12, 15 before 14), so the reader has to jump around to rebuild what actually happens when.

author: haiku
reason: B gives a one-line overview of the flow and then nine steps that run in the order they are written, each clear about what starts it, what moves, where state lives and what happens on failure; A spreads the same flow over 19 steps and also tells the reader to run some out of order (16 and 17 before 12, 15 before 14), so following it means jumping back and forth.

author: sonnet
reason: B is clearer for a newcomer because it opens with how the system works today, keeps the rollout sequence apart from the runtime mechanics, says where state lives at every step and ends with a failure summary table. A mixes runtime triggers such as process start and each /healthz call into its chronological build-and-rollout list.

author: sonnet
reason: A is easier for a newcomer to follow: it describes the current system first, keeps the ordered rollout separate from how the new code runs, and gives every step the same four parts (what starts it, what moves, where state lives, what happens on failure), while B puts runtime behaviour into the same numbered sequence with vague starting points like "when the code change is built" and has no "where state lives" field.

author: haiku
reason: A shows the stored state first and then walks through each flow with consistent numbered steps, branching diagrams and a failure table you can scan, while B's numbering is confusing ("steps 2 to 7" introduces a list that starts at an untransacted step 1) and it contradicts itself on failed sends ("Nobody is notified" against "raises an alert").

author: haiku
reason: B is consistent from start to finish: a summary up front, one ACTIVE rule, branching flowcharts and a failure table that gives the result, the link state and whether an email goes out for each case. A contradicts itself in places that would make a reader stop and second-guess: its worker section says nobody is notified on failure while failure path 4 says an alert is raised, and its step ranges do not match ('inside the transaction (steps 2 to 7)' starts with step 1, and the POST diagram says 4 to 9 while the notes say 6 to 8).

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier to follow: it opens with a component map, defines "token check" once and reuses it, and gives each flow a clean step list (with the reply sent before the lookup) plus a readable failure table, while A packs everything into one crowded code-block diagram whose arrows run across misaligned columns.

author: sonnet
reason: A starts with a one-line system map, the table and the shared "token check" definition, and then gives each flow as clean numbered steps (including the explicit reply-before-lookup ordering), whereas B's request diagram is cramped and misaligned, its arrows point at several columns at once, and its failure table sits inside a code block, so it takes more effort to read.

author: haiku
reason: Document A lays the flow out in grouped diagram sections and numbered steps in order, with a simpler state model (the state cookie holds the state value itself, the glink cookie holds the token) and compact state and failure tables. Document B's long glossary, topic-by-topic prose that repeats itself, and the extra layer of hashed keys (sha256 of state and of the flow cookie) make it slower to follow without making it clearer.

author: haiku
reason: A defines every term a newcomer to OIDC needs (PKCE, nonce, state, GETDEL, TTL), and its diagram source reads in flow order with each edge next to its node, so the engineer can follow it step by step; B has the crisper summary and numbered steps, but it leaves nonce and PKCE undefined, lists its diagram's nodes apart from their edges, and packs several steps into dense paragraphs.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives a newcomer an easier path through the design: a numbered overview, state grouped by where it is stored (PostgreSQL, Redis, cookies), and a flowchart split into labelled stages with colour-coded outcomes and a reading guide. A's single large ungrouped flowchart and its separate rules list cover the same ground but are slower to follow step by step.

author: sonnet
reason: A is easier to follow: a five-step summary comes first, and the flowchart is split into numbered sections (start, callback, settings, login, password loop) with a guide on how to read it, and every state store says when it is created and removed. B's terms and endpoint list are clearer, but its single flat flowchart puts the settings branch after the password loop, which makes the order of steps harder to follow.

author: haiku
reason: B explains its general terms (replica, snapshot, keyset paging, MERGE, lease) for a newcomer and draws one linear flowchart that matches its notes on triggers, data movement, state and failures, while A packs many preflight branches and manual-versus-scheduled rules into dense nodes and tangled edges that take far longer to work through, even though A covers more edge cases.

author: haiku
reason: Document A is easier to follow: it defines its terms first, its diagram reads in one straight line with clearly marked failure branches, and its notes lay out the trigger, data movement, state, failure and retry handling in plain separate sections; Document B makes the reader track a crowded diagram whose edges are listed apart from its nodes, plus nested preflight rules with exceptions for manual and timed-out runs.

author: sonnet
reason: B opens with a three-step extract, stage and commit summary and a list of what starts each piece of work, explains the lookback and upsert in plain terms, and keeps the failure table simple, so a newcomer gets the mechanism faster than from A, which has more edge cases (diagnostic attempts, manual re-runs, per-day reconcile transactions); B's lightly specified run lease is a smaller drawback.

author: sonnet
reason: A opens with a plain three-step summary (extract, stage, commit) and a trigger list, and its flowchart draws each data store and the reads and writes into it, so a newcomer can see what moves and where state lives sooner; B adds more ideas to keep in mind (the runner versus scheduler split, exit-code attempt counting next to an attempt number kept only for diagnosis, manual re-runs, per-day reconcile transactions with rechecks), which slows the first correct reading.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to follow for someone new to the stack: it opens with the goal, a flow diagram and a list of components, defines log, partition, offset and consumer-group terms, and uses a simple check-key, write, then set-key dedup with a ledger-based replay, whereas A's pending claims, compare-and-set takeover and 8-day lookback winner rule are dense and harder to trace step by step.

author: haiku
reason: Document A explains the generic terms an outsider needs (consumer group, acks = all, watermark, manifest), then gives numbered steps where it is clear what starts each one and where state lives (log, archive, KV key, ledger), and its live path and replay pick the first copy the same way; Document B relies on Kafka jargon it never explains and on a pending/committed claim takeover with compare-and-set and offset rules that is hard to follow, and its replay can pick a different winner than the live path.

author: sonnet
reason: A covers the same flow in one short numbered sequence, with each step's trigger and where its state lives, and it puts every failure case in a single table; B has a helpful diagram, but it spreads failure handling across many steps and adds machinery such as watermarks, a load ledger and straggler rules, so it takes longer to read and leaves more open to misreading.

author: sonnet
reason: A opens with a data-flow diagram of both paths and then walks through each component in order (collector, archiver, processor, loader, replay), saying what triggers each step and where state lives; B's single failure table is useful, but its replay-trigger, validation-override and KV-recovery rules are denser and harder to follow.
